title: FIRST $1,000 IN INDEX FUNDS: 6 THINGS TO KNOW
series_label: HOW TO INVEST YOUR FIRST $1,000 IN INDEX FUNDS: 6 THINGS TO KNOW

concepts.title: Why Index Funds First
concepts.body: An index fund holds every stock (or bond) in a market index in one ticker. S&P 500 funds own all 500 large US companies at once. You get instant diversification for the price of one trade — no stock-picking, no fund-manager guesses, low fees (0.03% for VOO).

visual_spec.callout_text: Index = one fund, hundreds of stocks. VOO owns 500 large US companies in one ticker at 0.03%. No picking, low fees, broad exposure.

concepts.title: What $1,000 Can Do
concepts.body: The S&P 500 has returned roughly 10% annually on average since 1928 — about 7% after inflation. $1,000 at 7% real return grows to about $1,970 in 10 years and $3,870 in 20 years (hypothetical, constant return). Not retirement money, but a real start. The point is the habit, not the headline number.

concepts.title: The Two Best Fund Picks
concepts.body: Two low-cost options cover nearly everyone: VOO (Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, 0.03%) and FXAIX (Fidelity S&P 500 mutual fund, 0.015%). Both hold the same 500 stocks. Pick VOO for any brokerage, FXAIX inside a Fidelity account to skip the broker fee.

concepts.title: Ups And Downs
concepts.body: Stocks don't go straight up. The S&P 500 has been positive in about 73% of calendar years since 1928 — so down roughly one in four. In any given year you might see +25% (2023, 2024) or −37% (2008), −18% (2022). The longer you hold, the more often good years outweigh bad ones. That's the deal.

visual_spec.callout_text: S&P 500 positive in about 73% of calendar years since 1928 — so down roughly one in four. Volatility is the price of the long-term return.

concepts.title: The 5-Step Plan
concepts.body: (1) Open a brokerage (Fidelity, Schwab, Vanguard). (2) Link your bank. (3) Deposit $1,000. (4) Buy VOO or FXAIX. (5) Set up an automatic monthly transfer — even $50 — to keep the habit. The first $1,000 is the hardest. The 100th is easy.

concepts.title: Don't Time The Market
concepts.body: Time in the market beats timing the market. The S&P 500 has been positive in about 73% of calendar years since 1928. The long-run return comes from staying invested through the bad years, not from waiting for the 'right' moment — most people who try to time end up missing the early-rebound days that drive the return.

visual_spec.callout_text: S&P 500 positive in ~73% of calendar years since 1928. Your $1,000 works hardest when it stays put. Automate and stop watching.
